entities.summary:
Polydor Records, established in 1913 in London, represents a significant chapter in the history of the music industry, particularly in the realm of popular music and recording technology. It became a key player in the evolution of the record label landscape, particularly in Western Europe, and is noted for fostering the careers of several prominent artists and bands, including The Who, The Doors, and Elton John. Its establishment coincided with the rise of the phonograph and the expansion of recorded music consumption, marking a pivotal moment in the cultural fabric of modern society.

Throughout its history, Polydor has produced numerous chart-topping hits and has been involved in groundbreaking music production techniques. The label played a crucial role in the British Invasion of the 1960s, during which British rock bands gained unprecedented popularity in the United States and around the world. Notably, Polydor was instrumental in the global success of The Beatles and other influential artists, significantly shaping the sound of the era. By the mid-20th century, Polydor had expanded its reach beyond the UK, establishing subsidiaries in various countries, thus facilitating the international distribution of its artists' music.

The legacy of Polydor Records is evident in its long-lasting impact on the music industry, influencing not only the artists it represented but also the broader landscape of popular music production and marketing. Many of the artists who emerged under the Polydor label have left a lasting imprint on music history, continuing to influence new generations of musicians. The label remains a symbol of the vibrant and ever-changing dynamics of the music industry, reflecting societal shifts and the evolution of taste in music. Polydor's contributions to the development of the music industry continue to resonate, as it has adapted to new technologies and trends, including the digital age of music.
